item.title: Do you really know｜为什么我们在压力之下会吃得更多？
item.description:
Why do we eat more when we're stressed?

Picture the scene. You've just got home after an absolutely awful day. You had to deal with urgent deadlines at work, a long commute, and bad news in your personal life. What's more, you've barely had a moment to yourself.

So you're at home, not particularly hungry, but still, you open the cupboard to see chocolate, biscuits and crisps in front of you. All of a sudden, you want to eat all of those snacks, no matter how calorific they might be. And it's not necessarily because you have a particular weakness for food. That stress you were dealing with. It can genuinely affect your appetite.

What's going on inside the body for that to be the case?

Well, it partly depends on the kind of stress we're experiencing. When we face an immediate threat, Our bodies release hormones including adrenaline, our hearts beat faster, our muscles tense up, and energy is directed towards dealing with the perceived danger. In that moment, eating may be the last thing on our minds. But when stress continues for longer, another hormone becomes important, cortisol, it helps the body mobilize energy and may also increase appetite.

Researchers at the University of Leeds published a meta analysis online in 2021, which combined 54 studies, involving almost 120,000 adults. It found that stress was associated with a small overall increase in food consumption. More specifically, it was linked to eating more unhealthy food and less healthy food.

However, there was considerable variation between people. In other words, stress can influence what and how much we eat, but it doesn't affect everyone in the same way.

Why is that tub of ice cream so much more tempting than a healthy option like carrots or broccoli?

Because eating isn't just about satisfying physical hunger. It can also activate the brain's reward system, particularly when foods contain plenty of sugar or fat. A review by researchers at the University of Geneva suggests that stress may make us more alert to cues associated with highly appealing foods. It can also strengthen automatic habits, and increase our motivation to obtain that food.

It's worth noting, that doesn't necessarily mean we enjoy it more. You might desperately crave some chocolate while feeling stressed, but actually experience no more pleasure from eating it than you normally would. Our routines matter too. If you regularly snack after a difficult day, your brain can gradually associate stress with food. Eventually, opening the biscuit cupboard becomes an almost automatic response.

But does comfort eating actually make us feel less stressed?

Not necessarily. In a 2019 American study called Cookie or Clementine, researchers put 150 women through a lab stress test. Some received foods that were high in sugar or fat. Some were given fruit or vegetables, and others received nothing at all. Neither healthy nor unhealthy comfort food significantly reduced participants psychological or physical stress responses compared with eating nothing.

So although food may feel comforting, the effect might come from expectation, distraction, or habit rather than the food actually reducing the body's stress response.

It's also important to remember that some people react in the opposite way and lose their appetite under stress. Ultimately, that craving after a difficult day doesn't always mean your body needs more energy. It may result from hormones, the brain's reward system and habits that have developed over time. There you have it.

item.title: BBC随身英语｜自助餐的安全隐患
item.description:
The dangers of buffets

The dizzying variety of options, the amazing range of flavours, and for some of us, the sheer quantity that you can eat. It's easy to see the appeal of a buffet. It takes the stress out of choosing what to eat - just have it all! But are there risks that we need to think about? Food hygiene specialists suggest there might be.

Restaurant and hotel buffets can be a food poisoning risk. The large number of different dishes and people serving themselves creates opportunities for cross-contamination. Microbes can be transferred from people to dishes, from dishes to people and from one dish to another. Even the air can transfer microbes to your food. It's easy to see how an entire buffet could end up contaminated.

Food temperature creates another risk factor. It's easy for food to be kept lukewarm and in the danger zone between 8C and 63C where bacteria and other microbes grow and multiply easily.

Restaurants that manage buffets well can reduce the risks. Hot food should be replaced after two hours and cold food after four. It's important that the old food is disposed of and that containers are not just topped up, allowing the older food to contaminate fresh items. Hot food should be kept above 63C, and cold food should be refrigerated.

However, any attempts by hospitality businesses to reduce risks can easily be undone by careless clients. There are many ways that diners can unwittingly or thoughtlessly increase the risks. Tongs and ladles can be contaminated by those who do not wash their hands, or who reuse their plates when getting a second helping. Food on display can be contaminated by people using the wrong utensil or who accidentally drop the handles into bowls of food. That's before even mentioning those who cough or sneeze near the buffet.

So, to enjoy a buffet, while keeping the risks as low as possible, you should check to see that it is well-managed by the restaurant or hotel, that others are following good hygiene rules and that you do the same. Even so, a buffet is likely to be more risky than other types of restaurants.

item.title: BBC六分钟英语｜我们能从不同世代身上学到什么？
item.description:
Learning from different generations

Phil

Georgie, do you often spend time with people who are much older than you or much younger than you?

Georgie

I do, actually, because I'm in a choir, so there's quite a wide range of ages – lots of older people, lots of younger people.

Phil

We can call an age group of people a generation. And you might feel that it's difficult to understand or agree with people from a different generation. Today on 6 Minute English, we're going to be finding out about a project that is gathering together the oldest people – that's those that are retired – with the youngest, and that's children who attend nursery. And we'll be asking the question, 'What can we learn from different generations?'

Let's start with our quiz question, Georgie. What generation would someone born in 1982 be in? Is it: a) Generation X, b) Millennial, or c) Gen Z.

Georgie

Phil, I'm going to go with Generation X.

Phil

OK. Well, we will find out the answer at the end of the programme.

Georgie

OK. Phil, so you said we're going to look at a project which gets small children interacting with older retired people. So, how does it work?

Phil

Well, in Chester, in the northwest of England, a nursery has opened up in a retirement village. There's the usual nursery staff to look after the children, but the older residents can join in for activities as well. There's a library, a cafeteria and a garden for the children and the older people to share, and some of the older people or 'grand-friends', as the children call them, lead some of the activities, like dance or crafts. And presenter of BBC World Service podcast People Fixing the World, Myra Anubi, went to visit the special nursery and spoke to some of the participants.

Myra Anubi

Ian was once a fighter pilot, and getting involved in the nursery has helped him fill a void.

Ian

It was after my wife died last year. It seemed I had a big, big hole to fill. And the people down in the nursery, they phoned me up and said, "We were doing such and such a thing. Why don't you come and join us?" And that's what I've been doing. So, yes, and I've enjoyed it. And I find it very interesting to see how they develop.

Myra Anubi

One of the things I heard from the grapevine is that you help the children make paper planes.

Ian

That's right.

Georgie

Myra says that the nursery helped Ian fill a void after his wife sadly died. If you fill a void, you find something to help you feel better after a loss.

Phil

Ian explains that after his wife died, staff at the nursery would phone him to tell him about the daily activities, which he refers to as such and such. And that's an expression that we use to talk about something without giving a specific example.

Georgie

It sounds like Ian has enjoyed spending time with the children at the nursery, and Myra tells him she's heard from the grapevine that he's been teaching the children to make paper planes.

Phil

Yes, hear from the grapevine is an expression, meaning that something is a rumour. And we also say, hear on the grapevine.

Georgie

Well, this nursery sounds like a really lovely project, Phil. What is the impact it's having on the older and younger people?

Phil

Well, the charity Ready Generations, which runs the nursery, says it works with universities to study the effects of mixing generations on health and wellbeing, and they say they've seen positive results. And there have been studies around the world on projects that encourage different generations to mix, and they found that they can help reduce loneliness, improve how healthy and well people feel, and even boost learning and creativity. And People Fixing the World host Myra spoke to Liz Ludden, co-founder of the nursery in Chester, about the differences that she's noticed since it opened.

Myra Anubi

And as I realised, these interactions also seem to be breaking down stereotypes.

Liz Ludden

Your first thought would be how lively and energetic young children can be, and what we found is so can older people. And so sometimes, you know, it's the older people that we're saying, "Can we just calm this down a little bit?"

Georgie

Myra says the nursery breaks down stereotypes. This means it provides evidence that common beliefs about a group of people are not true.

Phil

For example, a stereotype about generations is that younger people are lively, meaning they're loud and have lots of energy, whereas older people are not that lively.

Georgie

Right. But in the nursery, Liz says it's often the older people who have lots of energy and are being noisy rather than the children. The staff even have to tell them to calm down sometimes!

Phil

So, Georgie, is that something that you found in your choir?

Georgie

Actually, yes. The older people in my choir are big characters. It's often them who are dragging us all to the pub...!

Phil

OK. Georgie, I think it's time to look at the answer for that question. I asked if someone was born in 1982, which generation would they be from?

Georgie

I said Generation X.

Phil

OK. Well, actually, I'm afraid the answer was b) – they're a Millennial, just like you!

Georgie

Ah...! OK. Let's recap the vocabulary we learned in this programme, starting with generation, which is a group of people who are of a similar age.

Phil

Fill a void means find something to help you feel better after experiencing loss.

Georgie

Such and such is a way to talk about something without giving a specific example.

Phil

If you hear something on the grapevine, you hear a rumour.

Georgie

The expression break down stereotypes means find evidence that common beliefs about a group of people are untrue.

Phil

And lively means loud and with lots of energy.

item.title: BBC News｜“Mogging”当选柯林斯词典2026年度词汇
item.description:
'Mogging' is Collins' 2026 word of the year

Host: And before we go, towards the end of every year, different dictionaries announce their word of the year. Dictionary.com went first for 2026 with maxxing, and now the publishing house Collins has announced theirs. And Stephanie Prentice announced the news to Valerie Sanderson.

Stephanie: So Valerie, we're dealing with a slang noun here and it is... mogging. So Collins is defining mogging as the act of outshining or outperforming someone or something. So...

Valerie: No cats.

Stephanie: Sadly, no cats this time. But if you walked in this morning and I said, Valerie, you're mogging everyone in here, it means you look the best. It adds, though, that it can...

Valerie: I'm in for that.

Stephanie: Exactly. We need to start doing that. It adds it can make someone look inferior by comparison. So it's in terms of their appearance, their confidence, their status. It derives from an acronym, AMOG, so Alpha Male of the Group. and that's worth mentioning. It did originate in bodybuilding culture. It had connotations with the manosphere with toxic online culture.

But in 2026, it's seen this rapid mainstream adoption. So a 210% increase in usage. It is used now more broadly in a playful way by Gen Z and Gen Alpha.

Valerie: And is this different mogging to maxxing?

Stephanie: Different, but bedfellows. So maxxing short for maximising, doing something to the fullest or optimising it as much as possible. Like mogging, once seen as a bit toxic, now mainstream, so looksmaxxing, looking as good as you can, like you this morning. Sleepmaxxing, trying to get the best possible sleep.

Valerie: And does anyone older than Gen Z or Alpha, I mean, you do, but does anyone else know what these words mean?

Stephanie: It is a very good question, so we sent a Gen Z reporter out to ask a few people. So from the chats we've had in the office today and from those people on the street, research would suggest, no, not everyone knows what mogging means.

Valerie: And how do these words compare to last year's choices and did for many years ago?

Stephanie: Well, from the words we've had so far, so maxxing, mogging, in their current form, they do seem a bit more optimistic. So last year, for example, we had rage baiting. I'm sure you know what that is. It's basically annoying people on purpose.

Valerie: We had a lot of that in the office.

Stephanie: We all like a bit of that. We had parasocial. So it's an older word, but in this context, it's having a one-sided relationship online, maybe with a chatbot, a celebrity. We had slop, that low quality content we see. So given this is meant to capture the zeitgeist, maxxing and mogging could be seen as more positive. It's self-improvement, it's ambition, it's a greater sense of agency.

item.title: BBC随身英语｜为什么越是严肃的场合，越忍不住想笑？
item.description:
Why do we sometimes keep laughing at the worst times?

Do you ever find yourself laughing at the worst possible moment? A meeting at work, a serious ceremony, in the middle of a presentation? It's probably happened to all of us at some point. Now, here's the other thing. Have you ever noticed that when it happens, it's really hard to make it stop? It's also quite hard not to join in when someone else starts doing it. Just why do we get the giggles?

There are different types of laughter, and the giggles actually have their own system. Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience Sophie Scott describes different systems for producing laughter. Some laughter is easily controlled and used as part of conversation. This comes from a system linked to speech production.

However, the giggles are different. Scott tells us that the system used for involuntary, uncontrolled laughter is one that we share with other mammals. The shape that our vocal tracts make when we laugh in this way is different – less like speech, simpler, and more likely to produce whistling and squeaking sounds. Crucially, it also triggers our pleasure and reward systems. That might be why our brains don't really want to interrupt the process.

Awkwardly, it's even harder to stop the giggles when we're somewhere where we really shouldn't laugh. Professor of Anatomy Michelle Spear tells us that when we are in a solemn or serious situation where self-control is really important, our brains actively try to stop us expressing emotions.

The thing is, this is the same system that we use to control laughter. If there's a higher load on that system, then any laughter that bubbles out of us is going to be harder to get back under control. Also, thinking what we shouldn't be laughing about reminds us that we shouldn't be laughing about it, and that can keep us laughing about it.

Laughing is social, and that makes it even worse. When someone else starts laughing, we are likely to join in, and that's another thing that makes it hard to stop. One theory is that we evolved to laugh when something turns out not to be as dangerous as we thought, for example when what we thought was a dangerous predator is actually just a shadow. If everyone else joins with this, then the message gets spread wider. This is great for survival and evolution, but less useful when you can't stop laughing at a really awkward moment.

item.title: Do you really know｜为什么有些人总是爱迟到？
item.description:
Why are some people always late?

We've all been late at some point, but for some, tardiness is a chronic habit. You probably know someone who's always running behind, or maybe you're the one struggling to make it on time.

While it can be frustrating. Research shows that chronic lateness isn't just a matter of poor time management or lack of discipline. For some, it might even be linked to underlying psychological and neurological factors.

So what causes chronic lateness?

Several factors could be at play. For one, personality plays a big role. Take the optimist, for example. This person genuinely believes they can squeeze more into a limited time frame, only to find themselves rushing at the last minute. Then there's the perfectionist. Someone who checks and rechecks every detail, often losing track of time in the process.

Another culprit, people who have trouble saying no by overcommitting, they end up with a packed schedule that leaves little room for delays. And perhaps the most frustrating of all, the egoist, someone who simply doesn't consider how their tardiness affects others. For them, it's a matter of prioritizing their own time without regard for anyone else's.

Why don't they just look at the clock?

It's not that simple. Research shows people have different senses of time, and some are worse at estimating than others. Hugo Spires, a cognitive neuroscience professor at the University College London, found that students new to the city were more likely to underestimate travel time, especially when they were familiar with their surroundings.

This suggests that our brains rely on shortcuts, like past experiences, that can distort our perceptions of time, making us think we have more of it than we actually do.

What's going on in the brain of a chronic latecomer?

Chronic lateness may be linked to brain development. Research suggests that the prefrontal cortex, which helps with planning, may not be fully developed or functioning in habitual latecomers. Studies show, they often underestimate tasks, durations by up to 40%, factors like sleep deprivation or attention deficit disorder. ADD can also contribute to chronic lateness.

So can anything be done to change this?

The good news is it's possible to become more punctual. Author David Robson suggests visualizing your day and realistically estimating how long each task will take, setting phone alarms or reminders for each step can help you stay on track and adding a buffer, like an extra 15 minutes, can help you handle unexpected delays and reduce stress.

In short, while being late can feel like a habit, with some awareness and planning, it's definitely something you can improve. Next time you're running behind. Remember, your brain, not your willpower, might be the culprit. There you have it.

item.title: BBC随身英语｜如何在不牺牲地球的情况下享受时尚？
item.description:
Enjoying fashion without costing the planet

Social media brings influencer and celebrity culture to our phone screens, making it hard to resist the temptation of jumping on all the latest fashion trends. But when the fashion industry is responsible for up to 10% of global emissions, according to the UN, more than the temptation and shipping industry combined, we could all make an effort to make more conscious clothing decisions.

Most of the environmental impact comes from the use of raw materials – a huge amount of oil is needed to produce synthetic materials like polyester, for example. According to the waste charity Wrap, making a pair of jeans requires 10,000 litres of water! Many clothing companies have launched "eco" collections, using organic or recycled materials, but critic say this does not address the biggest problem – overconsumption. One rubbish truck of textiles is thrown away every second globally, according to the Ellen MacArthur Foundation. So, how can we have fun with fashion without costing the planet?

An answer usually given is to buy second hand. High quality items that might usually cost an arm and a leg at retail price can cost you a fraction. Though buying second-hand clothing is more sustainable than buying new, it often doesn't replace fast fashion habits, rather it supplements them.

One of the things we can do instead, writes professor of consumer psychology Cathrine Jansson-Boyd, is 'shopping your closet'. Creating new looks with existing pieces in your wardrobe can be a fun, creative process. She suggests setting yourself a ten-day challenge to wear combinations of your clothes that you have not worn before.

Another idea is to get comfortable with having fewer clothes. Decision paralysis may be a familiar feeling when you're getting ready in the morning and thinking 'What on earth am I going to wear?!' That problem falls away when you only have a few t-shirts to choose between. If decluttering your wardrobe feels negative, try a shift in mindset. Professional organiser Marie Kondo says it's not about choosing which items to get rid of, it's about carefully selecting the items which 'spark joy' – keeping only the items which speak to your heart. And for those items which you may only wear once for an occasion, try borrowing from a friend or renting.

Overall, we have many options at our fingertips, but if there's one takeaway, it's to avoid impulse purchases. If you find yourself wanting to buy the latest fashion trend, give yourself at least 48 hours to make the decision, and ask yourself, are there ways to avoid buying this new?

item.title: BBC News｜你扔掉的果蔬边角料，可能是纤维宝藏
item.description:
The hidden fibre in fruit and vegetable scraps

Host: Some food news for you now, and the revelation that eating the parts of fruits and vegetables that we often throw away could be an easy way to boost fibre in our diets.

Food scientists in Britain have found that peels, stalks, seeds and rind often contain more fibre than the parts of those foods we normally eat. Our health reporter, Michelle Roberts, told us more.

Michelle: They're talking about things like for a kiwi, if you eat the whole fruit, including the furry outside, that's going to give you about 50% more fibre than if you just ate the juicy middle bit on its own. Other examples are kind of using broccoli stalks, you might want to blend them, put them in soups or in stir fries.

And things like pineapple core can contain a lot of fibre. So if you were going to make a smoothie, you could include some of that. I mean, they do go as far as suggesting that pineapple skin is quite a good source. But one of the nutritionists I spoke to, she said it's not about trying to make people eat things that they really don't want to. It's just about thinking a bit more about what parts you might want to eat. But pineapple skin, she was less sure about.

Host: Even I sort of wrinkled my nose at the thought of having to do that. But, you know, what's the benefit of doing this? Why would we want to kind of try to be eating more of the things that we would normally throw in the bin?

Michelle: So this is all about fibre. we know that most people, most adults really don't get enough. And it's really important for your gut health. Fibre is great for helping everything transit through the body and go out the other end as it's needed.

And it's really linked to a lower risk of things like bowel cancer and heart disease. So digestive health is really important. And just getting enough fibre, so many of us just don't do it.

Host: And while we are all thinking about this, though, there are some things that we really shouldn't eat, right? Some seeds and some rinds and stalks and things. What should we be careful of?

Michelle: Yeah. So obviously wash things, you know, if you're going to put it in your mouth, make sure it's clean enough. But also there are certain things like if you've got rhubarb, the leaves of rhubarb are toxic. So don't go for something like that. But you can check first. You can do a bit of a Google search and just make sure that what you're thinking about eating is safe.

item.title: BBC News｜“Maxxing”当选Dictionary.com 2026年度词汇
item.description:
'Maxxing' is selected as Dictionary.com's 2026 word of the year

Host: What do 6-7, demure and hallucinate have in common? Well, they're all recent words of the year from Dictionary.com. The winner for 2026 has just been revealed, and it is maxxing.

The slang term's been added to a whole host of activities or attributes to indicate they've been optimised to the full. Popular examples include looksmaxxing, sleepmaxxing and even Catholicmaxxing. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth adopted the term lethalitymaxxing to describe the Pentagon's focus on killing.

But unlike other common viral trends, the word maxxing has actually been around for quite some time, according to linguist and author Adam Aleksic.

Adam: The word maxxing has been around since at least the 1970s in tabletop role-playing games, the idea of min-maxing your character for a certain stat. And then that was carried over to video game culture, and eventually on 4chan extended to the idea of yourself as a character. You can maximize your own stats.

So it's been around, but the modern usage of it absolutely popularized through social media. TikTok, particularly 2022, 2023 is when we start seeing this word hit the mainstream.

I wouldn't read too much into the word of the year. It's primarily a marketing event to sell more dictionaries. Last year, it's 6-7. I don't think that has a longstanding applicability, but maxxing is a suffix that we see productively applied to a lot of new words, and it does seem to have the potential to stick around.

But its entry into the dictionary canon doesn't really change how people are using it, I think. It's an interesting reflection of our society as a whole. I do think there's a trend toward optimization and maximizing that is reflected in this word. And it's a way to understand kind of more broadly what's going on in our culture right now. I think this drive toward optimization is one of the central tensions of modern society.

But you have to understand there's simultaneously a tongue-in-cheek aspect to the word maxxing. There's an ironic valence to it, where you could say, oh, I'm Chinamaxxing or I'm Catholicmaxxing. And that doesn't mean, like you're fully. It could be dangerous if you're lethalitymaxxing or if you're fibermaxxing and you do it to the point of ignoring other aspects, you optimize out the wholeness of this greater totality. But if you say it in kind of a funny way, that's all right. And I do think that's a common usage of the word.

item.title: Do you really know｜FOPO：“害怕他人看法”正在阻碍你吗？
item.description:
Is FOPO holding you back?

Have you ever really wanted to try something new, but avoided doing so because you were afraid of being judged, maybe pursuing a hobby that could be seen as uncool, wearing a flashy outfit, or sharing your opinion on a controversial topic, for example? Well, if that sounds familiar, then you might just be a victim of FOPO.

What does that stand for?

It's the fear of people's opinions. The concept was developed by psychologist Michael Gervais, who connected it to a very deep fear of rejection and warned that it could hinder personal growth, creativity, and authenticity by leading us to conform to societal expectations and seek external validation.

In 2023, He released a self-help book called the 1st rule of mastery. Stop worrying about what people think of you, providing strategies to overcome FOPO. Gervase has suggested that FOPO shows up in 3 stages.

First of all, anticipation. Before a social interaction, your brain overheats with a flood of thoughts and emotions, you start wondering what people might think of you and already fear judgment or criticism.

The 2nd stage is monitoring. You enter a phase of control and type of vigilance during your interactions. Every word is analyzed, and you're carefully watching people's reactions and body language. Looking for any signs of potential judgment, you become obsessed with the image you're projecting and don't fully experience the moment. Sometimes you even forget the name of the person you're talking to.

Finally, the 3rd stage is adaptation. And that might be the hardest one, because at this point, you can't really be yourself anymore, you're constantly adjusting your behavior to avoid rejection. For example, by laughing at a coworker's bad joke just to blend in.

Is having FOPO actually a problem then?

Well, in small doses, no, but when it becomes an obsession, that's when it becomes paralyzing. Just imagine how much energy you spend trying to be liked. It can be exhausting, both mentally and physically, with the constant fatigue increasing our mental load and leading to psychological distress.

It's important to recognize that our condition as social beings has existed since prehistoric times. Humans who are alone tended to have very low survival rates. The gaze of others could bring disapproval, which could lead to exclusion from the group, and that could, in turn, lead to death.

It's normal to have some anxiety before a social interaction. But when that stops you from acting and turns into social phobia, therapy might be something to consider. Small exercises to strengthen your self-esteem can be very helpful, especially to check whether the scenarios you fear so much actually happen. There you have it.

item.title: BBC随身英语｜咖啡文化正在发生怎样的变化？
item.description:
How is coffee culture evolving?

Coffee is one of the most popular drinks in the world. In Italy, espresso is often enjoyed quickly like a shot, whereas Scandinavian coffee culture places more emphasis on taking time to enjoy coffee socially.

In Ethiopia, which is often considered the birthplace of coffee, they take their coffee culture very seriously, and drinking coffee can last several hours. Freshly roasted beans are ground by hand, then brewed in a special clay pot before being served in small cups and enjoyed in three rounds, each round symbolising deeper community connection and blessing.

The way people drink coffee is rooted in tradition, but it's also changing. According to a BBC News article with the headline Coffee Price Surges to Highest on Record, coffee is the world's second most traded commodity by volume, and its popularity is increasing, perhaps because of new drinking cultures.

Drinking coffee doesn't just give you a boost of energy. It's been known to have some health benefits too. According to BMJ, a peer-reviewed medical journal, an analysis of nearly 220 studies found that coffee drinkers may enjoy more overall health benefits, such as a lower risk of specific cancers and neurological, metabolic, and liver conditions. Some young adults are also becoming more interested in coffee with additional health benefits.

Hardtank's research into Gen Z coffee trends suggests that young consumers are becoming more interested in health-conscious coffee, for those who actively care about physical, mental, and nutritional well-being. Drink Ripples also reports that 38% of consumers will pay more for drinks with added health benefits. Blends that use mushroom powder, proteins and collagen are also gaining popularity.

The drink also has to look the part. Pure Gusto's research into UK cafe trends highlights how customers want drinks that are more exciting. There has been a surge in using unusual ingredients with interesting flavours and creating colourful and fun aesthetics for drinks. Ingredients such as ube and black sesame are appearing in specialty drinks, while sweet and savoury combinations such as miso caramel are making traditional coffee more adventurous. These ingredients, along with toppings such as cold foam and cream, are becoming more popular.

So, how do you take your coffee? Are you more traditional in your method of preparing coffee with boiled water and perhaps a splash of milk or a bit of sugar? Or do you love mixing in syrups to create sweeter flavours and pouring your concoction into a clear cup and adding toppings to show off your coffee creativity?

item.title: BBC六分钟英语｜空调是应对全球变暖的答案吗？
item.description:
Is aircon the answer to a heating world?

Georgie

So, Neil, we've just had a really hot summer in the UK. Did you have air conditioning in your house?

Neil

I didn't have air conditioning in my house. I wish I had, because it was really hot and I couldn't sleep.

Georgie

No, I had one of those big fans, which didn't always do its job. But there is a really serious side to this. Heat records continue to be broken around the world. You may be feeling that summers are getting too hot. Have you been using air conditioning more to cope? If so, you're not alone. Experts are predicting that ten new air conditioning units will be installed every second for the next 30 years. Today on 6 Minute English, we're talking about this and whether air conditioning really is the best way to cope with a warming world.

Georgie

OK. As always, Neil, we'll start with a quiz question. So, modern air conditioning was invented in 1902, but what was it originally used for? Is it: a) to protect people in hospitals, b) to dry ink, or c) to clean air?

Neil

Well, I have absolutely no idea, Georgie. I'm going to guess and say c) clean air.

Georgie

OK, Neil, we'll find out the answer at the end of the programme.

Neil

OK. Georgie, we've been talking about how uncomfortable the hot weather can make you feel in the summer. Is air conditioning all about comfort, though?

Georgie

No, it's not just about comfort. Summer heat can be a real health issue as well. It's thought that across Europe, over 30,000 people died as a result of this summer's heat. Dr Radhika Khosla, an expert in climatology, told BBC World Service's The Climate Question how important air conditioning can be:

Dr Radhika Khosla

Actually, air conditioning is life-saving. You know, in Singapore, when Lee Kuan Yew was asked what made civilisation possible in the tropics, he said it was air conditioning. And there are so many large parts of the world where we would not be able to inhabit if we did not have air conditioning.

Neil

So, Radhika is saying that air conditioning is life-saving. It literally stops people from dying.

Georgie

Yes, and she makes the point that there are many parts of the world that we would not be able to inhabit – that means live in – without this technology.

Neil

OK Georgie. So, it sounds like air conditioning has a lot of good things about it. Is it all positive, though?

Georgie

No. There are some serious downsides. So, one big problem with air conditioning is the amount of energy it uses. Let's hear more from Radhika talking to The Climate Question:

Dr Radhika Khosla

When air conditioning becomes the first, go-to solution for how we deal with the increased, prolonged and extreme heat that we're going to face and are facing, it places stresses across the system that are not able to be met. So, you know, we're going to see the grid collapse. We're going to see emissions rise. We're going to see all kinds of other impacts that actually are quite detrimental.

And we reach a vicious cycle, because then you're in a world where it's getting warmer. We're using air conditioning to be able to protect ourselves. That's leading to more emissions and more energy use. That is then making the world warmer. And then we need more air conditioning.

Neil

We heard about the grid. The grid is the network that distributes electricity across towns, cities and countries. If people are trying to use more electricity than it can cope with, then the grid can collapse – you get power cuts, which is when you can't get any electricity.

Georgie

We heard that air conditioning creates emissions, which can lead the world to warm up, which means we then need more air conditioning. This makes the world even warmer and so on. And Radhika calls this a vicious cycle. A vicious cycle, or a vicious circle, is where a solution to a problem actually makes it worse, which means you have to do more and that makes the problem even worse still.

Neil

OK. Well, that sounds like a bit of a problem. What are the solutions?

Georgie

Well, Radhika says that there are some things we should try first before using air conditioning, which will still be important. Here she is again talking to The Climate Question.

Dr Radhika Khosla

So, one of the most important things is to do passive cooling first. Now, passive cooling is when we take steps to provide thermal comfort that are not energy intensive. Some of the most important ones are first to cut solar gain, which is through things like shading.

Neil

Passive cooling is where you cool your house down without using a lot of energy.

Georgie

Yes, heat from the sun can be blocked by shading, which could be with trees, curtains or blinds.

Neil

OK Georgie. So, passive cooling and shading – that sounds really easy. Is it that simple?

Georgie

No, that's not all we have to do. Radhika also talks about the importance of using sustainable energy to power the air conditioning that we still will need.

Neil

OK Georgie. It's time, I think, for you to give the answer to the question you asked us.

Georgie

Yes, Neil. I asked you what modern air conditioning was used for when it was first invented in 1902.

Neil

And I had a wild guess. I said c) to clean air. But you know what? I'm feeling pretty confident now.

Georgie

Sadly, you are incorrect. The correct answer was b) to dry ink. It was invented by Willis Carrier at a printing company in Brooklyn, New York.

Neil

OK. Let's recap the vocabulary we learned in this programme, starting with life-saving, which describes something that stops people from dying.

Georgie

If it's possible to inhabit somewhere, that means it's possible to live there.

Neil

The grid is the system or network that distributes electricity across towns, cities, and countries.

Georgie

A vicious cycle is where a solution to a problem also makes it worse, meaning the problem just keeps getting even worse as you try to fix it.

Neil

Passive cooling is where you make a building cooler without using a lot of power.

Georgie

And shading is blocking the sun's light and heat.

item.title: BBC News｜为什么欧洲最繁忙的购物街要“禁车”？
item.description:
Why is Europe's busiest shopping street going traffic free?

Host: Since the department store Selfridges opened a century ago, Oxford Street in central London has been the country's retail mecca. Hundreds of thousands of people visit there every day.

The omnibuses and horse manure might be a thing of the past in their place, cars, buses, taxis and lots of delivery vans. But not for much longer, because as of Monday, more than half of Oxford Street is going to be traffic free. So how will that work? My colleague Shaun Lay has been to meet someone in the know.

Shaun: I'm with Katie Morrison who is the Deputy Chief Executive of the Oxford Street Development Corporation. Katie, tell me what's planned along this stretch and what is after all, I think I'm right in saying, Europe's busiest shopping street?

Katie: It is indeed. And from this Monday, so that's the 26th of October, Oxford Street will become permanently traffic free. So from that day onwards there will be no buses, no taxis, no cycles on the street and instead it will be for pedestrians only for a one kilometre stretch from Great Portland Street to Orchard Street.

Shaun: Right, so traffic will still be able to cross Oxford Street at certain points?

Katie: It will indeed yes.

Shaun: But why are you doing this? I mean it's a hugely successful street, half a million visitors a day. And as we walk along here trying to avoid the umbrellas, I can well believe it, it's not broken, it doesn't need fixing.

Katie: Well, you're right. It remains a hugely popular street, but as you can see, it's not always the best shopping experience for people. It's crowded and the pavements are very busy.

And what we want to do is transform that. We want to make it somewhere that is much more positive experience, but also has many more elements to it. So as well as people being able to come and shop, especially in the run-up to Christmas, there'll be many more places to rest, to dwell, to eat your lunch, enjoy other activations happening around the street.

Shaun: There is traffic here at the moment. It's going to have to go somewhere.

Katie: Yes, we've been working very closely with Transport for London, who have been doing a huge amount of work over the last year to redirect the traffic appropriately and the buses. I'm very proud to say that new bus stops have been put in in a series of enabling works around Oxford Street.

Shaun: What about people who, for example, the elderly, people with disabilities? I think some disability activists have already expressed concern about this. at the moment they can get a bus or indeed a taxi right outside to the shop they want to go to. That's not going to be possible in the future.

Katie: You're right to raise that. It's been a really, really important issue for us and accessibility considerations have been at the heart of our thinking. We've taken great care to make sure that there's no bus stops more than 200 metres from the street and taxi ranks 100 metres from the street and no lost to Blue Badge spaces.

Shaun: How is it going to fare up in terms of competing with other global cities do you think if you pedestrianize Oxford Street?

Katie: Well, we have spent quite a lot of time as the Oxford Street Development Corporation talking to other cities that are doing similar schemes and we've learned a huge amount both in terms of the kind of economic impact but also some of the real practicalities. So for example, in Times Square they were very keen to point out the need to really maximise the use of additional seating, which we are doing as part of our plans.

We know that high streets are changing, they're changing around the world, and it's really important that London is ahead of that change and is spearheading a new way of shopping and a new way of experiencing retail, and Oxford Street will be at the heart of that.

item.title: Do you really know｜最常见的恐惧症有哪些？
item.description:
What are the most common phobias?

We've all got fears. For some, it's the dark. For others, it's spiders, heights, or maybe even something as ordinary as a phone call. But when those fears take root, and are no longer reasonable, when they take over, that's when they cross into the territory of phobias.

Phobias remind us that our brains, for all their brilliance, aren't always working in our favor and are flawed. According to a survey by Anxiety UK, there are 10 phobias that show up more often than the rest.

So what are these phobias?

Surprisingly, the number 1 spot isn't spiders or heights, it's social phobia. This is the fear of social interactions, and yes, that even includes telephonophobia, the fear of answering the phone.

Close behind is agoraphobia, the fear of open spaces. Think crowded concert venues where escaping feels impossible. At number 4, we have erythrophobia, the fear of blushing in public, which often overlaps with social anxiety, and claustrophobia, the fear of being trapped in tight spaces rounds out the list at number 10.

Are there any phobias related to animals?

Definitely, arachnophobia, the fear of spiders and zoophobia, the fear of animals, takes 8th and 9th spots. Zoophobia itself, covers several different fears. Cynophobia, the fear of dogs, ornithophobia, the fear of birds. Most animals are scary because they can bite or sting, but some are also associated with disease, such as rats.

And while we're on the subject of health, hypochondria, the fear of becoming ill makes the list too. Emetophobia, the fear of vomiting, or seeing someone else vomit, it actually lands at number 3. Believe it or not, some people even avoid nightclubs entirely because of it.

What else?

Transportation shows up in the rankings as well. In 7th place, there's aerophobia, the fear of flying, and in 5th, amaxophobia, the fear of driving.

The good news is that phobias don't have to rule your life. Treatments like cognitive behavioral therapy can help retrain the brain's reaction to fear. EMDR, a method that uses eye movements, works to reprocess traumatic memories. Hypnosis, on the other hand, goes straight for the unconscious. Seeking help does not mean erasing your fear entirely, but learning to stop letting it control you. There you have it.

item.title: BBC随身英语｜为什么开始锻炼如此困难？
item.description:
Why it is so hard to start exercising

Exercise. We know it's great, both for our physical and mental health, and it's one of the easiest ways to feel better. The recommendation for most adults is to do 150 minutes of moderate exercise a week. However, the UN has estimated that 1.8 billion people across the world don't manage to do this. So, what's stopping us?

We may have evolved to avoid exercise. According to evolutionary biologist Daniel Lieberman, because early humans needed energy for hunting, we developed an instinct not to waste this energy on seemingly pointless exercises. Of course, now our lifestyles have changed dramatically, but this instinct remains to some degree, pulling us towards our sofas. We naturally like to relax.

Often we have to fight against our habits. Many of us will have developed a habit of inactivity and changing this is hard. Psychologist Brad Stennerson tells us that some research shows it can take at least six weeks to make an exercise routine habitual. The good news is that once we make exercise a habit, it's a lot easier to keep going.

It may be that what we need to focus on are the cues that lead us to start exercising. This could be the time of day, or the start or finish of another activity. Psychology professor Alison Phillips calls this the instigation habit, and her research suggests that is key to develop an exercise routine. If you decide that you will do exercise as soon as you finish work, this may make it easier to stick to.

Let's not forget that exercise feels like hard work. And in fact, it's starting it that often feels the worst. This is because your muscles suddenly demand energy and your body has to work out where to get it from. Sport scientist Richard Taylor explains that it can take 10-15 minutes for your body to find an equilibrium and provide the muscles' needs easily.

One thing to remember is that exercise doesn't necessarily need to be highly intensive. The recent trend in South Korea for slow jogging, where people jog at a slow enough speed to chat comfortably, helps to remind us that big health gains can be found by moving from no activity to some activity.

If you're looking to start an exercise regime, most experts offer the same advice. Find something that you enjoy. Start with small goals and try to stay consistent. That makes it easier to build up a habit and before you know it, it will be part of your routine.

item.description:
"Disastrous" year of ice loss for Swiss glaciers

The notable finding here is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking, which is to be expected in our warming climate. What is extraordinary is the sheer pace of melting. Researchers estimate that Swiss glaciers released more than two trillion litres of water between July and September.

This ice lost to summer melting is far outpacing any gains from winter snowfall. Scientists say the sobering truth is that the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.

But researchers stress that sharp cuts to carbon emissions can still save much of the planet's glacier ice. They say this is crucial for the hundreds of millions of people worldwide who rely on the water from glaciers for farming, hydropower or drinking, as well as to limit sea level rise.

What should you eat for a better night's sleep?

Phil

Hi Georgie.

Georgie

Hi Phil. Now, Phil, do you ever struggle to get a good night's sleep?

Phil

You know, I do sometimes. If I've been thinking about something a lot, or even worse, if I've had a cup of coffee later than I should, sometimes I can lie there for hours.

Georgie

Yes. Well, many of us will be familiar with that feeling of lying in bed, feeling really tired, but just not being able to go to sleep, but what causes us to struggle to sleep and is there anything we can do about it? Well, researchers have for a while been interested in the link between what we eat and how we sleep. Today on 6 Minute English, we'll be talking about this and asking, "What should you eat for a better night's sleep?"

Georgie

OK. Phil, let's start with a quiz question. So, adults need between 7–9 hours sleep a night to stay healthy, according to experts, but what percentage of people in the UK say they get less than this? Is it: a) 15%, b) 25%, or c) 35%?

Phil

OK. I think people find sleeping hard, so I think it's going to be c) 35%.

Georgie

OK. Well, we'll find out the answer later in the programme.

Phil

Georgie, you've been looking at the research on this. Do scientists think that what we eat affects how we sleep?

Georgie

Yes, they do. Scientists have done some long-term studies. So, looking at large groups of people over a long period of time, and they found that a healthier diet is associated with better quality sleep. They've also done some smaller studies looking in more detail at exactly what people are eating and then studying how they sleep in a laboratory.

Phil

OK. And in these studies, have they found that particular foods are better for our sleep than others?

Georgie

Well, it's less about particular foods and more about particular nutrients. So, nutrients means important things your body needs to survive and be healthy. For example, protein is a nutrient. BBC World Service programme The Food Chain has been speaking to researcher Professor Marie-Pierre St-Onge about which nutrients are important for sleep.

Marie-Pierre St-Onge

So, diets that look more like a Mediterranean pattern – higher in fruits and vegetables, whole grains, lower in animal-based foods, lower in sugar. But then from our own research, where we evaluate food intakes in the lab, we see different... similar patterns, really. But when we talk about nutrients, diets that are higher in fibre, which we find in fruits and vegetables and whole grains, and lower in saturated fats, which we find in more plant-based types of foods, are associated with more deep sleep at night.

Georgie
